body:
The material still does not tell us what the recurring chores are, how long this has gone on, what the withdrawing flatmate has said, or whether the lease makes any arrangement easy to change. I would not treat the account's ambiguity/specification reading as established, and I would not treat the objection's renegotiation or legitimacy readings as established either. The rival adds a second axis that the account and the objection both underplay: the dispute may be about what kind of household the flat is, not only about what a chore agreement meant. I would keep the account's practical probes because they are cheap and can be run, but revise their order and their evidential weight.

What I now think is defensible:

1. Do not open with a shared note or a house meeting. Open with separate, bounded conversations, starting with the flatmate who is avoiding. Ask what they want the flat to be, what makes these conversations hard, and what would make recurring chores less fraught. Do not frame this as a prelude to a group settlement. The objection is right that a tighter spec on bins will not get a withdrawn flatmate back into the room; the rival is right that the form of the arrangement can itself be the contested thing.

2. From those conversations, form rival hypotheses rather than one diagnosis. The candidates are: ambiguity in what was agreed; renegotiation after schedule change; dispute about who has standing to raise or enforce; real or perceived load imbalance; conversational form or conflict fatigue; and a unit-versus-private-lives disagreement. These are distinguishable, but not from the original material alone.

3. Run one or two small probes, time-boxed to about a week. Probe A: take one recurring chore and write a minimal specification - what counts as done, by when, fallback if unable - as an experiment, not a contract. Probe B: try one low-exposure arrangement for one zone or rotation, with a default outcome no one negotiates in the moment. Record recurrence, but also record whether the item is replaced by a new complaint, whether a schedule change breaks it, whether resentment or avoidance changes, and whether the withdrawing flatmate engages with the content or pulls back from the idea of an arrangement. That last observation is the rival's most useful addition; it distinguishes ambiguity from a rejection of mutual obligation better than recurrence alone.

4. Interpret the probes carefully. Reduced recurrence with content-engagement supports ambiguity. Reduced recurrence with substitution, new complaint items, or schedule-triggered breakdown points toward renegotiation, load, or legitimacy. Pullback from the proposal itself points toward the unit-versus-privacy axis. No change, or worsening, points away from chores and toward the relationship or the living arrangement. I would not treat a drop in recurrence as confirmation by itself; the objection is right that the account's original test was too weak.

5. Set a checkpoint after two to four weeks. If no arrangement holds, if avoidance persists, or if the probes mainly generate new complaint items, name the lease and living-arrangement question explicitly. That does not force a move, but it stops a chore dispute from carrying a compatibility question indefinitely.

What I would avoid: a single big meeting to settle everything; moral language about pulling weight; counting instances in the moment; and treating a written spec as neutral when the rival's point is that it can enact one reading of the household without having settled it. Truce-shaped arrangements should also be watched for the opposite failure: they can shield a flatmate who simply will not do a fair share. A minimal shared baseline, such as not leaving common areas unusable, is worth keeping in view.

The strongest thing I can say is that the next move should be diagnostic and small. The account supplies a usable probe but overcommits to one hypothesis. The objection correctly weakens that probe's evidential force and shifts attention to conversation form. The rival supplies the missing second axis and a better distinguishing observation. None of them settles what is actually happening.

If no arrangement holds, avoidance persists, or the probes mainly produce new complaint items, shift the question from chores to whether the living arrangement still fits.","action":"Name the lease and living-arrangement question explicitly rather than letting a chore dispute carry it indefinitely.","consequence":"Puts the larger decision on the table without forcing it from a single chore disagreement.","depends":["cl1","ob1"]},{"id":"cm1","type":"commitment","text":"If tightened specification on a recurring item reduces recurrence and the withdrawing flatmate engages with the content, continue lightweight specifications for recurring items and revisit them when schedules change.","scope":"Contingent on use2 showing content-engagement and reduced recurrence without substitution.","depends":["use2","cl2"]},{"id":"cm2","type":"commitment","text":"If the withdrawing flatmate pulls back from the idea of a written arrangement rather than from its content, shift to the unit-versus-privacy axis and try truce-shaped arrangements before proposing more specifications.","scope":"Contingent on use2 or use3 showing pullback from the arrangement form.","depends":["use2","use3","cl3","cl4"]},{"id":"cm3","type":"commitment","text":"If no arrangement holds or avoidance persists at the checkpoint, name the living-arrangement question explicitly and stop treating the problem as a chore-specification problem.","scope":"Contingent on use4 checkpoint being reached without a workable arrangement.","depends":["use4","ob1"]},{"id":"p1","type":"problem","text":"The material does not identify the recurring chores, how long the pattern has lasted, what the withdrawing flatmate has said, whether the lease allows changes, or whether load imbalance is real. The probes can clarify some of this locally but cannot settle the diagnosis in advance.","mentions":["cl1","use2","use3","use4"]}],"uptake":["cl1","cl2","cl3","cl4","ob1","ob2","use1","use2","use3","use4","cm1","cm2","cm3"]}
